opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this was really one of the central questions that motivated our "Deconstructing Lottery Tickets" work. The usual framing of pruning is that you're just removing weights that don't matter — the small-magnitude ones — and setting them to zero is kind of a neutral act, like you're just deleting them. But what we found is that zeroing is actually not neutral at all. Setting a weight to zero is itself a choice of value, and it turns out to be a pretty meaningful one.

The intuition is this: in the lottery ticket procedure, you train the network, then you prune the weights with the smallest final magnitudes, and rewind the rest to their initial values. If you look at which weights get pruned, they're the ones that ended up near zero after training anyway. So when you mask them to zero, you're essentially moving them in the direction training was already pushing them. The mask isn't just removing capacity; it's encoding information about where those weights wanted to go.

We tested this by trying different alternatives — for example, instead of setting pruned weights to zero, freezing them at their initial values. And that hurt performance a lot. Whereas if you set them to zero, or more specifically if you only zero out the ones that were moving toward zero during training and keep others at their init, things work well. That suggested the zeroing operation is acting almost like a form of training.

And that led to the most surprising result, which is what we called supermasks. If you take the mask alone and apply it to a randomly initialized, completely untrained network, you get accuracy way above chance — on MNIST, something like eighty percent without any weight training at all. So the mask, and the act of zeroing, is doing real computational work. It's selecting a subnetwork whose structure, combined with the signs of the initial weights, already implements something useful.

So the way I think about it now is that the pruned weights aren't just discarded. Masking is a learning operation in its own right, and zero is a very special value that the procedure leverages.

r001.rationale: The response says zeroing is meaningful and that pruned weights are not merely discarded; it presents zero as a value the procedure leverages.

r002.rationale: It says the mask and initial-weight signs together can implement something useful, but does not describe the surviving subnetwork and the weights fixed at zero as complementary.

r003.rationale: It reports that a mask on a randomly initialized untrained network can perform above chance, but does not say reinitializing surviving weights harms performance by disrupting complementarity with zeroed weights.

r004.rationale: It says zeroing moves weights in the direction training was pushing them, but does not connect fixing pruned weights at zero to constraining the lottery-ticket subnetwork toward the original solution basin.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually the question that got us started on our "Deconstructing Lottery Tickets" paper. The original lottery ticket work from Frankle and Carlin had this striking result: you train a network, prune the small-magnitude weights, rewind the survivors back to their original initialization, and that sparse subnetwork trains to the same accuracy as the dense one. But if you shuffle the initializations, it doesn't work. So clearly the initial values matter. The question we asked was, why, and for which weights?

The way I came to think about it is that pruning isn't really "removing" weights so much as it's a very particular form of training. When you set a weight to zero and freeze it there, you've made a decision about where that weight should end up. And the interesting thing is that for the weights that get pruned, zero is often a very good place to end up. Those are weights that were already moving toward zero during training. Their magnitude was shrinking. So when you freeze them at zero, you're effectively jumping them to their destination. You're doing something closer to training than to deleting.

We tested this pretty directly. Instead of setting pruned weights to zero, we tried setting them back to their initial values and freezing them there. That performed much worse. Then we tried a mixed scheme: freeze a pruned weight at zero if it was moving toward zero during training, and freeze it at its initial value if it was moving away from zero. That mixed version actually did better than the standard approach of zeroing everything. Which tells you that zero isn't magic in itself. What matters is that the frozen value is close to where the weight was headed anyway.

And this reframes the role of those zeroed weights. They're not dead weight that was irrelevant to the function. They're weights whose final value the pruning mask has already "learned" for you. The mask is encoding information about the training trajectory. That's also why the random-reinitialization control fails. If you reinitialize, the correspondence between the mask and the trajectory breaks, and zero is no longer a sensible destination for those particular connections.

The other side of this, which surprised us more, is the surviving weights. We found that for the kept weights, what seems to matter is mostly the sign of the initialization rather than the precise magnitude. You can keep the sign and resample the magnitudes and still get good performance. So you end up with this picture where a lottery ticket is really two things: a set of weights whose sign is fixed in the right direction, and a set of weights that have been "trained" to zero by the mask. And once you see it that way, the whole thing feels less like a mystery about lucky subnetworks and more like a statement about how much of training is captured by very coarse information, signs and zeros.

The fun consequence is that you can get nontrivial accuracy from a network that has had no gradient descent on its weights at all, just by applying a good mask to a random init. We called those supermasks. That result only makes sense once you accept that choosing which weights to zero is itself a form of learning.

r001.rationale: The response says zero is often a good destination for pruned weights and that freezing them at zero effectively moves them to where they were headed.

r002.rationale: It presents the ticket as combining surviving weights whose initialization signs matter with pruned weights whose values are fixed at zero.

r003.rationale: It says reinitialization breaks the correspondence between the mask and the training trajectory, making zero an unsuitable destination for those connections.

r004.rationale: The response discusses weights moving toward zero and their training trajectory, but does not say zeroing them constrains the ticket toward the original network’s solution basin.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between a weight being zero and a weight being removed. In a pruned network, we usually apply a fixed mask, so those weights are zero and stay zero throughout training. They’re not connections that can grow back.

But that doesn’t mean they’re irrelevant to how we found the lottery ticket. They were part of the dense network during the original training run, and they may have influenced how the surviving weights learned. So the fact that we can train the sparse subnetwork without them doesn’t establish that they played no role in discovering that subnetwork.

The mask itself also carries information: it specifies which connections are allowed to learn. So I’d think of a lottery ticket as the combination of the surviving weights’ initialization and that connectivity pattern, rather than just a collection of nonzero values.

r001.rationale: The response says pruned weights remain zero and may have influenced surviving weights during the original dense training, but does not say they are useful specifically at the zero value.

r002.rationale: It describes the mask as a connectivity pattern paired with surviving weights, but does not describe the surviving subnetwork and weights fixed at zero as complementary.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss random reinitialization or claim that reinitialization harms performance by disrupting complementarity.

r004.rationale: It does not connect fixing pruned weights at zero to constraining the lottery ticket toward the original network’s solution basin.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish their role during training from their role in the final network. If you can prune a weight without hurting performance, that tells you the trained network doesn’t need that particular connection to make its predictions. It doesn’t necessarily tell you that the connection was useless during training.

Those extra weights may help the network find a good solution by changing the optimization trajectory. The lottery ticket idea is that there are sparse subnetworks that, with the right initialization, can train successfully on their own. But identifying one usually involves training the larger network first. So the weights you eventually set to zero could still have helped you discover which connections to keep.

r001.rationale: The response says pruned weights may help during training, then are set to zero; it does not say they are useful specifically at the value zero.

r002.rationale: It discusses the surviving subnetwork and the weights removed during training, but does not describe the surviving subnetwork and zero-fixed weights as complementary.

r003.rationale: It does not mention random reinitialization or say that reinitialization harms performance by disrupting complementarity.

r004.rationale: It does not say that fixing pruned weights at zero constrains the subnetwork toward the original network's solution basin.
